metadata.title: INTERVIEWERS, TEST-TAKING CONDITIONS AND THE QUALITY OF THE PIAAC ASSESSMENT

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper uses PIAAC Survey of Adult Skills data from the 2012 and 2015 rounds (first and second waves) and analyses country-level variation in test-taking conditions and interviewer effects. The reported empirical strategy relies on OLS regressions at the individual level with country averages shown for some models, and on econometric decomposition of interviewer effects on response rates and engagement measures. The manuscript does not report the use of PIAAC sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so it is unclear whether complex survey design adjustments were applied in the estimation. Because the study focuses on data-quality indicators (disengagement, length complaints, response rates) rather than PV-based achievement modelling, the paper’s weighting transparency is limited; analysts using PIAAC microdata should apply the standard PIAAC sampling weights when estimating population-representative quantities.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This working paper does not model cognitive achievement scores using PIAAC plausible values; instead, it analyses engagement/attention indicators derived from the cognitive assessment process (disengagement) and an interviewer observation measure (length complaint), plus response rates. Because the dependent variables are non-PV quality indicators, plausible values handling is not applicable to the main analyses. The paper also does not document a missing-data strategy for these indicators (e.g., how cases with missing paradata or missing engagement components were treated), so missing-data handling is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper uses PIAAC Survey of Adult Skills data from the 2012 and 2015 waves across participating countries/economies (33 total participants mentioned overall). For the engagement measure 'disengagement', the indicator can only be computed for respondents who took the computer-based assessment because timing information is unavailable for paper-based respondents; the paper notes that this applies to 72% of respondents. For models of engagement and length complaints, the analyses are conducted at the individual level but some results are shown as country averages due to small country-level sample sizes. The manuscript does not provide a detailed list of additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., specific missing-data exclusions or paradata completeness thresholds).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper examines whether variation in PIAAC test-taking conditions and interviewer practices threatens the validity of cross-country comparisons. Using PIAAC paradata collected by interviewers (room of assessment and observed distractions/interruptions) and interviewer-linked indicators, the study describes substantial between-country differences in assessment environments and in interviewer assignment size. It then relates these variations to engagement/attention measures: (i) 'length complaint' (whether the respondent complained about interview length) and (ii) 'disengagement' (based on whether respondents failed to attempt at least 10% of assigned cognitive items, using computer-based timing). The results indicate that room-of-assessment and recorded interruptions are unlikely to create meaningful cross-country quality differences, while interviewer assignment size and interviewer effects may have only mild impacts. The paper also highlights limitations: no causal identification is attempted, and missing-data/paradata recording issues constrain deeper interviewer-effect analysis.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD working paper focused on survey quality and measurement validity using descriptive statistics and OLS/econometric decomposition of interviewer effects rather than machine-learning prediction. As a result, there is no ML model training/evaluation, no PV-based achievement outcome, and no structured ML target-variable findings to tabulate. The paper also does not report a total analytic sample size or per-country student counts in the provided text, so total_students and n_students remain unavailable.
